Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impression:
  - Adult with type 2 diabetes presenting with 3–4 months of progressive, painful, cracked, dry, intermittently itchy palms that started after changing to housekeeping work involving frequent exposure to cleaning products and inconsistent glove use. E45 emollient and an oral antihistamine have been ineffective. Patient systemically well, no fever reported.  
- Working diagnosis (supported by transcript and DDx): 
  - Irritant contact dermatitis (occupational hand dermatitis) — working diagnosis (High likelihood). Rationale: classic temporal association with new housekeeping role and repeated exposure to cleaning agents without gloves; palmar distribution with fissuring and pain; supported by DDx.  
- Relevant differentials from DDx (supporting/refining impression): 
  - Allergic contact dermatitis — Medium likelihood (sensitization to cleaning product chemicals or glove components possible; pruritus prominent).  
  - Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection) — Low–Medium likelihood (chronic palmar scaling/fissuring possible; diabetes increases fungal risk).  
  - Palmar psoriasis and diabetic xerosis noted by DDx but considered less likely given strong occupational correlation (see considerations).  
- Management plan documented in transcript and consistent with DDx:
  - Immediate measures given/documented:
    - Avoidance of triggers: strongly advised to wear gloves when cleaning at all times.  
    - Emollient therapy: use stronger emollients liberally, recommended 3–4 times daily (patient instructed).  
    - Topical steroid: clinician stated a steroid cream will be prescribed and prescription sent to patient's pharmacy — specific agent/dose/route/frequency not documented.  
    - Return and follow-up: if no improvement in ~1–2 weeks or earlier if worsening/spreading, patient to re-attend.  
  - Additional considerations supported by DDx (to consider if not improving or if atypical features develop):
    - Evaluate for secondary bacterial infection if increased erythema, purulence, systemic symptoms, or worsening pain/fever.  
    - Consider fungal testing (KOH microscopy/culture) if poor response to treatment or clinical suspicion of tinea manuum.  
    - Consider patch testing or dermatology referral if allergic contact dermatitis suspected or dermatitis persists despite avoidance and topical therapy.  
- Conflicts or uncertainties:
  - No direct physical examination findings or objective skin description documented (physician discussed diagnostic impression but did not document lesion morphology beyond patient report).  
  - No laboratory or imaging data available.  
  - Conflict noted: none between transcript and DDx; DDx supports the clinician's impression.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Irritant contact dermatitis (occupational hand dermatitis) — High. 
  - Justification: Strong temporal relationship to job change with repeated exposure to cleaning agents and inconsistent glove use; palmar cracking, dryness and pain are classical features and clinician reached same impression.  
- Allergic contact dermatitis — Medium. 
  - Justification: Occupational exposures to multiple chemicals/rubber accelerators may cause delayed hypersensitivity producing pruritic, fissured palms; consistent with pruritus and occupational history.  
- Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection) — Low–Medium. 
  - Justification: Chronic scaly, fissured palmar lesions can be fungal; diabetes increases fungal risk though no foot infection or characteristic borders were reported.
